notes.title: Files – revision sheet
notes.md:
## Opening and modes
- `FILE *fp = fopen("data.txt", "r");` – check `fp == NULL`; `fclose(fp)` flushes and frees
| Mode | Meaning |
|---|---|
| "r" | read; NULL if missing |
| "w" | write; erase or create |
| "a" | append; create if missing |
| "r+" | read + write; must exist |
| "w+" | read + write; erase or create |
| "a+" | read + append |
- Add **b** for binary ("rb", "wb"); text mode may translate newlines (\n ↔ \r\n on Windows)
- Text vs binary: 12345 → 5 characters vs 4 raw bytes
- Standard streams: stdin, stdout, stderr

## High-level (stream) functions – <stdio.h>
- Character: fgetc/getc, fputc/putc (store in int; EOF = −1); strings: fgets(buf, n, fp), fputs
- Formatted: fprintf, fscanf; blocks: fread/fwrite(&rec, sizeof rec, 1, fp) (return the item count)
- Position: fseek(fp, offset, SEEK_SET/SEEK_CUR/SEEK_END), ftell, rewind (= fseek(fp, 0, SEEK_SET)); feof, ferror, fflush, remove, rename
- Record k (1-based) starts at (k − 1) × sizeof(rec); file size: fseek to end, then ftell

## Low-level (UNIX system calls)
- open(name, O_RDONLY / O_WRONLY / O_RDWR | O_CREAT | O_APPEND, 0644) → int fd; read(fd, buf, n) (0 at EOF, −1 error); write; lseek; close
- fd 0, 1, 2 = stdin, stdout, stderr; unbuffered

## Command line arguments
- `int main(int argc, char *argv[])`; argv[0] = program name; argv[argc] = NULL
- `./prog one two` → argc = 3; quoted text is one argument; convert numbers with atoi/atof

notes.title: File handling – detailed notes with worked examples
notes.md:
## Opening and closing
```c
FILE *fp = fopen("marks.txt", "r");
if (fp == NULL) { perror("marks.txt"); return 1; }
/* … use the file … */
fclose(fp);
```
| Mode | Meaning | If the file does not exist | If it exists |
|---|---|---|---|
| "r" | read | returns **NULL** | read from start |
| "w" | write | creates | **erases** (truncates) |
| "a" | append | creates | writes at the end |
| "r+" | read + write | NULL | keeps content |
| "w+" | write + read | creates | erases |
| "a+" | read + append | creates | reads anywhere, writes at end |
Add `b` for binary files: "rb", "wb", "ab+". On Windows text mode turns "\r\n" into "\n" when reading.

## Reading and writing functions
| Level | Read | Write |
|---|---|---|
| character | `fgetc(fp)` / `getc` → int, EOF at end | `fputc(c, fp)` / `putc` |
| line / string | `fgets(buf, n, fp)` (keeps the '\n'; NULL at end) | `fputs(s, fp)` (no newline added) |
| formatted | `fscanf(fp, "%d", &x)` | `fprintf(fp, "%d\n", x)` |
| block / binary | `fread(ptr, size, count, fp)` | `fwrite(ptr, size, count, fp)` – both return items done |

## Moving around
- `fseek(fp, offset, origin)` – origin `SEEK_SET` (start), `SEEK_CUR` (current), `SEEK_END` (end)
- `ftell(fp)` – current position in bytes; `rewind(fp)` = `fseek(fp, 0, SEEK_SET)`
- File size: `fseek(fp, 0, SEEK_END); long n = ftell(fp);`
- `fseek(fp, -10, SEEK_END)` – 10 bytes before the end; `fseek(fp, sizeof(struct rec) * 2, SEEK_SET)` – third record

## Standard programs
```c
/* copy a file character by character */
int ch;                                   /* int, not char – EOF is -1 */
while ((ch = fgetc(src)) != EOF)
    fputc(ch, dst);

/* count characters, words and lines */
int c, chars = 0, lines = 0;
while ((c = fgetc(fp)) != EOF) { chars++; if (c == '\n') lines++; }

/* write and read a structure */
struct rec { int id; float m; } r = {1, 88.5f};
fwrite(&r, sizeof r, 1, fp);
rewind(fp);
fread(&r, sizeof r, 1, fp);
```

## Other functions
- `feof(fp)` – true only **after** a read has hit the end; `ferror(fp)` – error flag; `clearerr(fp)`
- `fflush(fp)` – write out the buffer; `fclose` flushes too (data may be lost if a program crashes before closing)
- `remove("a.txt")`, `rename("a.txt", "b.txt")`, `tmpfile()`
- Standard streams opened automatically: **stdin, stdout, stderr** (`fprintf(stderr, "error\n")`)
- EOF is a macro (usually −1) in `<stdio.h>`; from the keyboard: Ctrl+Z (Windows) / Ctrl+D (Linux)

## Text vs binary files
| Text | Binary |
|---|---|
| human-readable characters | raw bytes as in memory |
| numbers stored as digits ("12345" = 5 bytes) | an int is 4 bytes |
| fprintf / fscanf / fgets | fwrite / fread |
| newline translation (Windows) | none |

## Traps
- `while (!feof(fp)) { fgets(...); print }` prints the **last line twice** – test the return value of the read instead
- `char ch = fgetc(fp)` may never equal EOF if char is unsigned → infinite loop; use `int`
- Opening with "w" destroys the old content
- Always check `fopen` for NULL; always `fclose`
- `FILE` is a structure type defined in `<stdio.h>`; `fopen` returns `FILE *`

notes.title: KRIES syllabus word by word – Files
notes.md:
> **Syllabus:** File operating modes, text and binary files, high-level and low-level operations on files, command line arguments

### File operating modes
- **Means:** the second argument of `fopen` that says how the file is used.
- **Key facts:** `"r"` read (file must exist, else NULL), `"w"` write (creates or **erases**), `"a"` append (creates, writes at end), `"r+"` read/write (must exist), `"w+"` read/write (erases), `"a+"` read/append; add `b` for binary (`"rb"`, `"wb+"`).
- **Example:** `FILE *fp = fopen("data.txt", "a");`
- **Exam point:** opening an existing file with `"w"` deletes its contents.

### Text files
- **Means:** files of readable characters arranged in lines.
- **Key facts:** numbers stored as digit characters (12345 → 5 bytes); newline may be translated (`\r\n` on Windows); functions `fprintf`, `fscanf`, `fgets`, `fputs`, `fgetc`, `fputc`.
- **Example:** `fprintf(fp, "%d %s\n", roll, name);`
- **Exam point:** text files are portable but larger and slower to parse.

### Binary files
- **Means:** files storing data exactly as in memory (bytes).
- **Key facts:** int always 4 bytes; no newline translation; `fread`, `fwrite`; good for records/structures, images.
- **Example:** `fwrite(&rec, sizeof rec, 1, fp);` · `fread(&rec, sizeof rec, 1, fp);`
- **Exam point:** fread/fwrite return the number of **items** (not bytes) transferred.

### High-level operations on files
- **Means:** buffered, stream-based I/O through `FILE *` (stdio.h) – portable.
- **Key facts:** `fopen`, `fclose`, `fgetc/fputc`, `fgets/fputs`, `fprintf/fscanf`, `fread/fwrite`, `fseek` (SEEK_SET/CUR/END), `ftell`, `rewind`, `feof`, `ferror`, `remove`, `rename`.
- **Example:** `fseek(fp, 0, SEEK_END); long size = ftell(fp);`
- **Exam point:** always check `fp == NULL`; `fclose` flushes the buffer.

### Low-level operations on files
- **Means:** unbuffered, system-call I/O using integer **file descriptors** (UNIX `<fcntl.h>`, `<unistd.h>`).
- **Key facts:** `open(name, O_RDONLY | O_WRONLY | O_CREAT …, mode)` returns an int fd; `read(fd, buf, n)`, `write(fd, buf, n)`, `lseek(fd, off, whence)`, `close(fd)`; standard fds 0 (stdin), 1 (stdout), 2 (stderr).
- **Example:** `int fd = open("a.txt", O_RDONLY); n = read(fd, buf, 100); close(fd);`
- **Exam point:** high-level = `FILE *` + buffering; low-level = `int` descriptor, no buffering, faster for big blocks, less portable.

### Command line arguments
- **Means:** values typed after the program name, received by `main(int argc, char *argv[])`.
- **Key facts:** `argc` = count **including** the program name; `argv[0]` = program name; `argv[argc]` = NULL; all arguments are strings → convert with `atoi`, `atof`.
- **Example:** `./copy a.txt b.txt` → argc = 3, argv[1] = "a.txt", argv[2] = "b.txt".
- **Exam point:** `./sum 4 5` → `atoi(argv[1]) + atoi(argv[2])` = 9.
